title: Process standards: time, capacity and Little's Law
sub: Lecture 5 + practice Test 1 · time you have vs time you need, capacity, OEE, TMU, Little's Law
blurb: How much time you have, how much you need, when an order must start, and the three numbers of Little's Law.
lede: The second and fourth exercises of Test 1. Two different questions: how much time do you HAVE, and how much do you NEED? The ratio tells you whether the capacity is enough. Little's Law links units, rate and time.
six: Two questions: how much time do you **have** (watch time − shift time) and how much do you **need** (unit time · units + batch time).
**Shift time** (breaks, cleaning) belongs to the shift, not to the order. Some of it may be written outside the table.
Never divide a **batch time** by the units: 4 cakes baked in 20 min is not 5 min per cake.
**Capacity** = the **maximum** output in a period. need / have: 100 % ideal, above it over capacity.
The answer is never 'we can't': it is '**we finish at…**'.
**Little's Law**: units in the system = rate · time. Two numbers are given, find the third, and watch units vs batches.
foot: Sources: 3BE216 lecture slides 'Process Standards', practice Test 1 (exercises 2 and 4) and its answer key, Lecture 5 and the Little's Law lecture as recorded.

questions.q: The time you HAVE in one 8-hour shift with 30 min of cleaning is…
Cut 20 WS25 (3.5 min each) and 100 WS30 (3 min each), setup 20 min per batch. Time you NEED?
Need 410 min, have 450 min. Need / have =
4 pieces are baked together for 20 minutes. Unit time?
questions.answer: There is none: 20 min is a batch time, one piece also needs 20 min
questions.e: Don't divide a batch time by the units.

questions.answer: the maximum output an operation can produce in a given period under given conditions
wrong: the time needed for one unit
questions.e: The answer must contain the word maximum.

wrong: the total time of one process
the time of one unit through the whole line
questions.e: Lead time: one unit start to finish. Cycle time: one process. Changeover: setup. Takt: the customer's rhythm.

questions.answer: the total time to complete one unit of a product or service
wrong: the time of one machine cycle

questions.q: A human-based operation needs 30 people. How do you plan it?
questions.answer: About 33–34 people: plan at 80 %, keep a buffer
questions.e: From the lecture: never plan humans at 100 %.

questions.q: IT shuts the servers down from noon to 1 pm. Which loss is that?
questions.e: Losses: personal (illness), technical and organizational, force majeure.

questions.q: Q3: 92 days, 10 shutdown days, 26 weekend days, 3 holidays, 2 shifts × 8 h, 5 h maintenance a month. Available time?
How many TMU in one hour?
In OEE, which losses separate operating time from net operating time?
questions.answer: Idling, minor interruptions and reduced speed
questions.e: Total → planned (−shutdown) → operating (−failures, settings) → net operating (−idling, minor stops, reduced speed) → productive (−defects, rework, losses from start).

questions.q: Need 1 965 min, have 458 min per shift. Shifts needed?
questions.e: 1 965 / 458 = 4.29: 4 full shifts plus 133 minutes on the first day.

questions.q: The order needs 133 min on its first day. The shift ends at 17:00, the last 17 min are cleaning. Start at…

questions.answer: units in the system, rate and time
questions.e: Three numbers: you get two, you find the third.

questions.q: 10 customers, one barista takes 5 min per customer. Serve all in 25 min: how many baristas?
questions.e: Needed rate: 25 / 10 = 2.5 min per customer; 5 / 2.5 = 2 baristas.

questions.q: 10 finished goods per day wait 2 days before shipping. Inventory?
8 000 transactions/hour, response time 5 s, think time 30 s. Concurrent users?
20 codes are in an office, 4 leave per day. A new one arrives. When is it ready to go out?
questions.e: time = units / rate = 20 / 4. It is ready to go out, not yet out.

vocab.meaning: Time tied to the shift, not the order (cleaning, breaks). You don't have it.
Time needed once per batch or order (setup, drawings, handing over).
Time that repeats for every piece.
Total time to complete one unit of a product or service.
Total time of a specific process.
The rate of the line's outputs.
The maximum output of an operation in a given period under given conditions.
Overall equipment efficiency: total time minus the losses down to productive time.
Specification range divided by the natural variation (±3 standard deviations).
Full-time equivalent: how many people working 100 % your workforce equals.
Predetermined motion time systems, such as MTM and MOST.
Units in the system = rate · time.
A loss nobody can control (a flood).

facts: In a human-based operation, plan at about {80|100|50|120} % so you keep a buffer.
Capacity is the {maximum|average|minimum|planned} output in a period.
Takt time is the rate of customer {demand|supply|service|complaints}.
Changeover time is another word for {setup|lead|takt|cycle} time.
Cleaning the workplace at the end of the shift is {shift|unit|batch|lead} time.
The answer to a capacity problem is never 'we can't' but 'we {finish|start|stop|wait} at…'.
Little's Law: units in the system = rate · {time|price|cost|capacity}.
